passages.title: When the Reef Turns White
passages.passage: Not until the summer of 1998 (1)____ marine biologists fully grasp how quickly a reef can die. That year an unusually strong El Niño pushed sea temperatures a degree or two (2)____ their normal maximum across much of the tropics, and reefs from East Africa to the Maldives lost their colour within weeks. The colour, it turns out, was never the coral's own. It belongs to microscopic algae living inside each polyp, (3)____ supply their host with most of its food in exchange for shelter. Under heat stress the polyp expels them, and the bare white skeleton shows through the tissue. A bleached coral is not yet a dead one; provided (4)____ the water cools soon enough, the algae can return and the partnership resumes. What worries researchers is the frequency (5)____ which these events now occur. A reef that once had a decade to recover between heatwaves may now have three or four years, hardly enough for slow-growing species to rebuild. (6)____ it not for a handful of unusually tolerant colonies, some reefs would already have vanished altogether. Scientists have begun cross-breeding these survivors in the hope of producing corals able to cope (7)____ warmer seas, though nobody pretends this will work at the scale required. Reef tourism, on (8)____ many island economies depend, is watching nervously. (9)____ the scale of the damage, one might expect bleaching to dominate environmental news; in fact it receives far less attention than deforestation. Only when a reef has gone entirely (10)____ people tend to notice what they have lost.

questions.explanation: Not until at the start of a sentence forces inversion with an auxiliary: Not until 1998 did biologists grasp. Have or could would need a different verb form and would not match the past-tense narrative.
Temperatures rise above (or over, beyond, past) a maximum. Than is tempting after 'a degree or two' but needs a comparative such as higher, which is absent.
A non-defining relative clause after a comma takes which for the algae. That cannot follow a comma in a non-defining clause, and who is reserved for people.
Provided that introduces a condition: on condition that the water cools. If or when cannot follow provided, which already carries the conditional meaning.
Events occur with (or at) a certain frequency, so the relative clause is the frequency with which they occur. In and by do not collocate with frequency.

Were it not for is the inverted form of if it were not for, an unreal condition whose result is would already have vanished. Was is not used in this inverted subjunctive, and Had would need had it not been for.
The phrasal verb is cope with a difficulty. In would describe where the corals live, not what they can withstand, and cope never takes to.
The preposition is fronted before the relative pronoun: tourism, on which economies depend. That can never follow a preposition, and whom is only for people.

Given (or considering) the scale of the damage means 'taking it into account', which is what leads one to expect heavy coverage. Despite would reverse the logic: the expectation follows from the damage rather than in spite of it.

A fronted Only when clause triggers inversion in the main clause: only when it has gone do people notice. Then is a tempting filler but leaves the sentence without the required auxiliary before people.

passages.title: Penny Universities
passages.passage: Legend has it that coffee was discovered by an Ethiopian goatherd (1)____ animals grew unusually lively after chewing red berries from a certain bush. Whatever the truth of the tale, the drink had reached the ports of Yemen by the fifteenth century, where Sufi monks used it to stay awake (2)____ their night-time devotions. From there it travelled north to Cairo, Damascus and Istanbul, and it was in these cities that the coffee house (3)____ such was born. Unlike the tavern, it sold nothing that clouded the mind; unlike the mosque, it demanded no particular conduct. Men of every rank could sit for hours over a single cup, playing chess, listening to storytellers or, (4)____ the authorities feared most, discussing politics. Several sultans tried to (5)____ the coffee houses down, and each time they reopened within months. When the habit reached London in the 1650s, it (6)____ hold with astonishing speed: by 1700 the city is thought to have had several hundred such establishments, each one attracting its own clientele. Merchants gathered at one, poets at another, and it was out of a coffee house near the Thames (7)____ the insurance market Lloyd's eventually grew. A penny bought admission and a cup, which is (8)____ the coffee houses came to be called 'penny universities'. Their decline in the eighteenth century, historians agree, had (9)____ to do with the quality of the coffee, which had if anything improved, than with the rise of private clubs and the growing popularity of tea. (10)____, the idea they embodied — a public room where strangers could talk as equals — has never quite gone away.

questions.explanation: Whose links the goatherd to his animals as a possessive relative: a goatherd whose animals grew lively. Who would leave animals without a possessor and produce two subjects in a row.
The monks stayed awake during (or through, throughout, for) their devotions, a period of time. While is a conjunction and needs a clause with a verb, not a noun phrase.
As such means 'in the proper sense of the word': the coffee house as such, as opposed to earlier informal gatherings. Like or for cannot combine with such here.
What the authorities feared most is a nominal relative clause standing for 'the thing they feared most'. Which would need a noun before it to refer back to, and there is none.
The phrasal verb close down (or shut down) means to stop a business operating. Put down or break down do not apply to an establishment, and ban does not take down.
A habit or idea takes hold when it becomes established. Got or caught hold would mean physically grasping something, which is not the sense here.

This is a cleft sentence: it was out of a coffee house that Lloyd's grew. Which is wrong because the emphasised element is a prepositional phrase, not a noun that a relative clause could modify, and where would double the place meaning already given by out of.
Which is why (or how) introduces the consequence of the penny price: it explains the nickname. Because cannot follow which is, and that would not express the reason.

Less to do with X than with Y ranks the two causes, and the aside 'which had if anything improved' rules out the coffee as the reason, so less is the only logical choice. More would make the improved coffee the main cause of the decline.

The final sentence contrasts the decline of the coffee house with the survival of its idea, so a concessive linker such as Nevertheless, however or yet is needed. Therefore or Moreover would present the survival as a consequence or an addition, not a contrast.

passages.title: Rebuilding the Past
passages.passage: Most of us imagine memory (1)____ a kind of recording, stored somewhere in the brain and played back on demand. Neuroscientists have spent decades demonstrating that nothing could be (2)____ from the truth. A memory is not retrieved so much as rebuilt, assembled afresh each time from fragments scattered across different regions, and every rebuilding introduces small changes. This explains why two people (3)____ witnessed the same event can give sincere but contradictory accounts of it years later. It also explains why memories can be planted: tell someone often (4)____ that they once got lost in a shopping centre as a child, and a surprising number will eventually 'remember' the episode in vivid detail. Sleep plays a role that was underestimated (5)____ recently. During the deeper stages of the night, the hippocampus appears to replay the day's experiences to the cortex, gradually transferring (6)____ has been judged important into long-term storage. Deprive a student of sleep after a day of revision and (7)____ of what was learned will be lost by morning. Forgetting, meanwhile, is not simply a failure of the system (8)____ part of its design. A brain that kept everything would drown in irrelevant detail, unable to tell a lasting principle from a passing coincidence. Had our ancestors remembered every leaf on every tree, they might never (9)____ recognised the one that was poisonous. The art of memory, in (10)____ words, lies less in holding on than in knowing what to let go.

questions.explanation: Imagine X as Y means to picture X in the form of Y. Like is tempting but after imagine it would compare memory to a recording rather than define what people take it to be, and to be is two words.
Nothing could be further from the truth is a fixed expression of strong denial, and British usage also allows farther. Far is not comparative, and away would need further in front of it.
A defining relative clause about people takes who (or that): two people who witnessed the same event. Which is not used for people, and whom is wrong because the pronoun is the subject of witnessed.
Often enough means 'sufficiently often', with enough following the adverb it modifies. Too would have to come before often and would give the wrong meaning, and very cannot follow the adverb.

Until recently marks the end point of the period during which the role was underestimated. Since would mean the opposite, that the underestimation began recently, and before is not used with recently in this way.
What has been judged important is a nominal clause meaning 'the things that have been judged important', and whatever is also possible. Which or that would need a noun before them to refer to.

A quantifier is needed before of what was learned: much, most, some, part or half. Many is wrong because what was learned is uncountable, and all overstates a claim the passage presents as a partial loss.
Not simply X but Y corrects one description with another: not a failure but part of the design. And would make forgetting both a failure and a design feature, and rather would need but rather here.

The inverted third conditional Had our ancestors remembered requires a perfect modal in the result: might never have recognised. Had after might is impossible, and be would make the sentence passive without an agent.
In other words signals that the writer is restating the argument more simply. Another is singular and cannot precede the plural words, and short would be in short without words.

passages.title: A Light with No One to Keep It
passages.passage: For the best part of two centuries, the lights (1)____ guarded Britain's coast were tended by men who lived beside them. The job was passed from father to son more often than (2)____, and a keeper's children grew up knowing the rhythm of the lamp better than the rhythm of the school bell. On the rock stations — towers built straight out of the sea, miles from the nearest land — three men would share a space no larger than a modest flat for weeks (3)____ end. Boredom was the enemy quite (4)____ much as the weather. Keepers carved, knitted, built ships in bottles, and kept diaries in which the arrival of the relief boat is recorded with an enthusiasm normally reserved (5)____ great victories. No sooner had a storm blown itself out (6)____ the men would be scrubbing salt from the glass, since a dirty lens could dim the beam by a third. The relationship between keepers and the ships they protected was oddly one-sided: sailors depended on the light absolutely, yet few of them ever gave a thought to (7)____ was up there keeping it lit. Automation began in the 1960s and was complete by the end of the century, (8)____ which point the last keepers were quietly pensioned off. Some welcomed retirement; others, (9)____ to the solitude, found the noise of ordinary life almost unbearable. Today the towers still stand and the lamps still turn, but nobody watches them do it. (10)____ many of the old keepers, that is the saddest part: a light with no one to keep it.

questions.explanation: A defining relative clause identifies which lights are meant: the lights that guarded the coast, and which is equally correct without a comma. Who is impossible because lights are not people, and what cannot introduce a relative clause after a noun.

More often than not is a fixed phrase meaning 'usually'. Ever would give more often than ever, a comparison with the past that makes no sense for an inherited job, and never is not used in this idiom.
For weeks on end means for many weeks without a break. At or in do not form this idiom, and without end would need a different structure.

The comparison of equality is as much as, here strengthened by quite: boredom was quite as much of an enemy as the weather. So is used only in negative comparisons (not so much as), and too would need too much without the following as.
Something is reserved for a purpose or occasion: enthusiasm reserved for great victories. To would suggest handing the enthusiasm over to the victories, and on does not collocate with reserved.
No sooner had ... than is the inverted pattern for two events in quick succession. When belongs with hardly had ... when, and then is a spelling trap that turns the sentence into nonsense.

After the preposition to, the clause who was up there is a nominal clause acting as its object, so who (or whoever) is the subject of was. Whom is tempting after a preposition but is wrong because the pronoun is a subject, not an object, and which is not used for people.
At which point means 'and at that moment', a relative phrase with a fronted preposition. By or from would imply a deadline or a starting point rather than the moment the pensioning happened.

Accustomed to (or used to, attached to) the solitude explains why ordinary noise became unbearable. Adapted to the solitude is possible in isolation, but the contrast with those who welcomed retirement points to habit, and keen or fond take on and of, not to.

For (or to) many of the old keepers introduces the people in whose view something is true. With would describe accompaniment, and Among would need a different verb, since that is the saddest part among them does not work.

passages.title: Roads That Held an Empire
passages.passage: Long before the Romans laid their first paved mile, other civilisations had learned that (1)____ a state could move its soldiers and grain, it could hold its territory. The Persians built a royal road stretching some 2,500 kilometres from Susa to the Aegean, along (2)____ relays of mounted messengers could carry a message in a week that would have taken a traveller on foot three months. The Inca, (3)____ had neither the wheel nor iron tools, nevertheless strung more than 30,000 kilometres of roads across the Andes. Their routes came complete with rope bridges swaying above gorges and storehouses spaced a day's walk (4)____. It is the Romans, however, (5)____ roads have left the deepest mark on the modern map. Their engineers dug a trench, packed it with layers of stone, gravel and sand, and finished the surface with a slight curve so that rain would run (6)____ rather than pool. So well were these roads made (7)____ several remain in use two thousand years later, and the routes of countless European motorways still follow them. What is often forgotten is the cost (8)____ which they were built. Much of the labour was carried out by soldiers between campaigns, and much of the rest by slaves and conquered peoples who had little choice (9)____ the matter. A road, in other words, was never simply a convenience; it was a statement that the land it crossed now belonged to (10)____ had built it.

questions.explanation: The clause states a condition: if (or once, when, where, provided) a state could move its soldiers, it could hold its territory. Unless would reverse the logic, and that is already used before the blank and cannot be repeated.

The preposition along is fronted before the relative pronoun for the road: along which messengers could carry. That can never follow a preposition, and where would clash with along, which already gives the place meaning.
A non-defining relative clause after a comma about a people takes who. That is impossible after a comma in this type of clause, and which is not used for people.
Things placed at regular intervals are spaced a certain distance apart. Away would need a reference point (away from something), and between cannot end the phrase without an object.

In this cleft sentence the emphasised noun the Romans is linked to roads by the possessive relative whose. Who would leave roads as a second subject with no connection, and that would make the Romans, not their roads, leave the mark.
Water runs off (or away from) a curved surface instead of collecting on it, which is the contrast with pool. Out would mean the rain was used up, and down alone leaves unclear where it goes.

So well were these roads made that is the inverted form of so ... that, expressing result. Which cannot introduce the result clause, and as would turn the sentence into a comparison with no second term.

Something is built at a cost, so the relative phrase is the cost at which they were built. For is tempting because we pay for things, but the idiom for a price or sacrifice is at a cost, not for a cost.
The fixed phrase is to have little choice in the matter. About or over can follow choice in other contexts, but the idiom with the matter takes in.

Whoever had built it is a nominal clause meaning 'the people who had built it', and whoever is the subject of had built. Whomever is a common trap after the preposition to, but the case is decided inside the clause, where the pronoun is a subject, and who alone cannot follow a preposition in this sense.

passages.title: The Dance in the Dark Hive
passages.passage: In the early twentieth century an Austrian zoologist named Karl von Frisch (1)____ out to discover how a honeybee returning from a rich patch of flowers manages to tell her sisters where it is. He painted tiny dots on the backs of individual bees and watched them for hours through the glass wall of an observation hive. (2)____ he saw was a dance. A forager that had found food close to the hive ran in a tight circle, turning first one way and then the other; one that had flown further performed a figure of eight, waggling her abdomen (3)____ time she crossed the middle line. The length of the waggle, von Frisch worked out, corresponds to the distance of the food, and the angle of the run relative to the vertical comb tells the others the direction (4)____ the sun. The system is (5)____ precise that bees can be sent to a dish of sugar water several hundred metres away that none of them has ever seen. Not everyone was convinced. Critics argued that the bees were simply following a scent picked (6)____ from the dancer's body. It took decades of increasingly ingenious experiments, including a robot bee that danced without any scent at all, to (7)____ the matter beyond reasonable doubt. Von Frisch was eventually awarded a Nobel Prize (8)____ the work, sharing it in 1973 with two other pioneers of animal behaviour. (9)____ the dance can properly be called a language remains a matter of definition, since it has no grammar and refers only to the here and now. Even so, it is the only known case (10)____ a creature other than a human passes on abstract information about something that is out of sight.

questions.q: Blank (1): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: Set out to do something means to begin with a definite aim. Put out means to extinguish or publish, made out means to manage to see, and took out means to remove.

questions.q: Blank (2): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: What he saw is a nominal clause meaning 'the thing he saw' and acts as the subject of was. Which and that need a noun to refer back to, and whatever would wrongly suggest that anything at all he saw counted as a dance.

questions.q: Blank (3): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: Each time she crossed means on every crossing. All the time would need the and means continuously, whole needs the whole time, and same would need the same time as.

questions.q: Blank (4): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: We speak of the direction of a landmark: the direction of the sun. To is used after verbs of movement (fly to), at after verbs of pointing, and for would mean 'on behalf of'.

questions.q: Blank (5): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: So precise that is the result pattern with an adjective. Such needs a noun (such a precise system), too would need to and would give the wrong meaning, and very cannot be followed by a that clause.

questions.q: Blank (6): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: A scent is picked up from a surface, meaning detected or acquired. Picked out means chosen, picked off means removed one by one, and picked over means sorted through.

questions.q: Blank (7): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: The collocation is put a matter beyond doubt. Set and lay are tempting because they also mean 'place', but neither forms this idiom, and bring would be bring into doubt, the opposite meaning.

questions.q: Blank (8): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: A prize is awarded for an achievement. Of would express possession, while on and about would describe the subject of a talk or book, not the reason for an award.

questions.q: Blank (9): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: A clause acting as the subject of remains must begin with whether. If can replace whether only after a verb, never as the subject of a sentence, and although and unless would leave the main verb without a subject.

questions.q: Blank (10): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: After case a relative clause describing a situation takes where, equivalent to in which. Which and that would make the creature's action into a description of the case itself with no preposition, and what cannot follow a noun.
